plain_english: Could you find a more miserable city than Athens when thirty tyrants were tearing it apart? They killed thirteen hundred citizens — all the best people — and they didn't stop there. The cruelty just made them hungry for more violence. This was the city with the sacred Areopagus court, with a Senate, with a popular assembly that was like another Senate. Now a gang of butchers met there every day. The unhappy Senate House was packed with tyrants. When a state has so many tyrants that they could form one man's bodyguard, you'd think it would give up the fight. It seemed impossible for people to even imagine getting their freedom back. They couldn't see any way out of such a massive evil. Where could this wretched state find enough heroes like Harmodius to kill so many tyrants?
original_excerpt: Could you anywhere find a [more] miserable city than that of Athens when it was being torn to pieces by the thirty tyrants? they slew thirteen hundred citizens, all the best men, and did not leave off because they had done so, but their cruelty became stimulated by exercise. In the city which possessed that most reverend tribunal, the Court of the Areopagus, which possessed a Senate, and a popular assembly which was like a Senate, there met daily a wretched crew of butchers, and the unhappy Senate House was crowded with tyrants. A state, in which there were so many tyrants that they would have been enough to form a bodyguard for one, might surely have rested from the struggle; it seemed impossible for men's minds even to conceive hopes of recovering their liberty, nor could they see any room for a remedy for such a mass of evil: for whence could the unhappy state obtain all the Harmodiuses it would need to slay so many tyrants?

plain_english: Look at Socrates. He lived right in the middle of the city. He comforted the grieving leaders and gave hope to those who had given up on the republic. He shamed wealthy men who were afraid their riches would destroy them, making them regret their greed. He walked around as a living example for anyone who wanted to follow his lead. He was a free man even though thirty tyrants ruled over everyone else. But Athens still killed him in prison. Even Freedom herself couldn't stand the freedom of a man who had mocked a whole gang of tyrants. This shows you that a wise person can make their mark even in an oppressed state. But in a successful, thriving state, arrogance, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices take control.
original_excerpt: Yet Socrates was in the midst of the city, and consoled its mourning Fathers, encouraged those who despaired of the republic, by his reproaches brought rich men, who feared that their wealth would be their ruin, to a tardy repentance of their avarice, and moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters. However, Athens herself put him to death in prison, and Freedom herself could not endure the freedom of one who had treated a whole band of tyrants with scorn: you may know, therefore, that even in an oppressed state a wise man can find an opportunity for bringing himself to the front, and that in a prosperous and flourishing one wanton insolence, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices bear sway.

plain_english: So we should adjust ourselves based on what the times demand and what Fortune offers us. But either way, we must keep moving — not freeze up from fear. The best person is one who faces danger, weapons, and chains on all sides but still doesn't hide or weaken their virtue. Staying safe doesn't mean burying yourself alive. I think Curius Dentatus was right when he said he'd rather be dead than truly alive. The worst thing of all is to stop living before you actually die. But if you happen to live in times when serving the state is nearly impossible, then it's your duty to spend more time on rest and learning. Think of it like sailing in dangerous waters — sometimes you need to pull into harbor and step away from public life before it forces you out.
original_excerpt: We ought, therefore, to expand or contract ourselves according as the state presents itself to us, or as Fortune offers us opportunities: but in any case we ought to move and not to become frozen still by fear: nay, he is the best man who, though peril menaces him on every side and arms and chains beset his path, nevertheless neither impairs nor conceals his virtue: for to keep oneself safe does not mean to bury oneself. I think that Curius Dentatus spoke truly when he said that he would rather be dead than alive: the worst evil of all is to leave the ranks of the living before one dies: yet it is your duty, if you happen to live in an age when it is not easy to serve the state, to devote more time to leisure and to literature. Thus, just as though you were making a perilous voyage, you may from time to time put into harbour, and set yourself free from public business without waiting for it to do so.
